to_subject.sentence: A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash.

“The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product,’” Topic said.

This scraping, Meta says, is for users’ benefit, feeding into Meta research into products to “help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services,” the
Following tweaks, it’s good that Meta added “more language about the permitted uses,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, told Nieman Lab.

What would help—as University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel told Nieman Lab—would be if Meta added specific language to the policy where the company agrees to respect scraping instructions in robots.txt files.

to_others.sentence: Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, told Nieman Lab that “publishers should remain concerned.”
But “[the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through,” he said.
When it comes to robots.txt, “you can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” Sobel said.
“Publishers must be able to decide whether and how their journalism is used, and negotiate fair payment,” the group’s executive director, Angela Mills Wad, said.

Similarly, Danielle Coffey, the president and CEO of the News/Media Alliance—which Nieman Lab noted is the largest news publishing trade association in the US— protested the terms as “outrageous and probably illegal.”
“It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30,” Coffey said.

to_others.sentence: Over the past two and a half years, we’ve reported on many of the ways in which threat actors tried to use our models to conduct cyber attacks, covert influence operations (IO), scams, and other violations of our Usage Policies.
One fake that the operation claimed to have planted in Peru even fed into public tensions between Ukraine and Poland.
In two cases, the evidence ties the operators to public reporting on “Politology.” The operators reported that, in 2024, they ran two campaigns targeting Argentina’s President Javier Milei.
Second, they claimed that they paid local actors to post anti-Milei graffiti in Buenos Aires.
For example, the operators claimed that in May 2026, they created a fake email address purporting to come from the Regional Directorate of Education in Lima, Peru.
According to the operators, some schools replied to the fake email address, confirming that they had held such events and even providing pictures.

unnamed.sentence: In their internal reports, the operators claimed to have spread fake stories across Latin America to undermine Ukraine or local leaders.

Some of these fakes have been attributed by open-source ⁠ (opens in a new window) researchers ⁠ (opens in a new window) to a Russian entity known as “Politology” or “La Compania,” a reported successor to the Wagner Group and other entities founded by Russian oligarch Yevgeniy Prigozhin.
Some described efforts to trick locals into carrying out activities that the operators could weaponize; others described fake “leaks” that the operators claimed to have spread.
First, they said they spread a false report that Milei had bought Cartier jeweled collars for his dogs.
According to their reports, this social media activity ran into problems when operators in different parts of the world tried to access the same accounts, leading to account restrictions.
According to their reports, the solution was to create more fake accounts to follow the first one and make it look more convincing.
